title: Pride and Prejudice - Chapter XIII
author: Jane Austen
description: The introduction of Mr. Collins, the heir to Longbourn, brings a unique blend of pompomus servility and self-importance to the Bennet household. His letter of reconciliation, laden with deference to Lady Catherine de Bourgh, sets the stage for his formal and awkward interactions with his cousins. The chapter masterfully explores themes of inheritance, social hierarchy, and the absurdity of religious and social performance.
summary: Chapter XIII metadata follows a strict 7-7-7 contract with superscript-labeled analysis, Renaissance-consistent image prompts with two prompt variations per scene, and callout-ready memorable quotes anchored for deterministic replacement.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mr. Bennet's blunt announcement of Mr. Collins's arrival forces the family to confront the reality of the entail. Mrs. Bennet's irrational hatred of the legal arrangement highlights her lack of systemic understanding, viewing it as a personal cruelty rather than a common patriarchal structure. Her emotional reaction serves as a foil to Mr. Bennet's detached, almost amused irony regarding their future displacement.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: in favour of a man whom nobody cared anything about.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mr. Collins's letter is a masterpiece of sycophancy, where every expression of goodwill is tied to his association with Lady Catherine de Bourgh. His claim to promote 'the blessing of peace' is undercut by his constant reminders of his status as the heir, creating a tone of condescending atonement. This rhetorical style perfectly captures the 'mixture of servility and self-importance' that Mr. Bennet so eagerly anticipates.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: not lead you to reject the offered olive branch.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Elizabeth's immediate identification of Collins as an 'oddity' demonstrates her superior judgment and wit. While Jane searches for credit in his intentions and Mary analyzes his composition, Elizabeth pierces through the formal language to find the underlying pomposity. Her skepticism marks her as the primary lens through which the reader is meant to view Collins's absurdity.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: There is something very pompous in his style.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The physical description of Mr. Collins as a 'tall, heavy-looking young man' with 'grave and stately' air reinforces his lack of natural social grace. His formal manners are not an expression of genuine respect but a rigid adherence to a self-constructed persona of clerical dignity. Austen uses his heavy presence to contrast with the lighter, more agile wit of the Bennet sisters.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: His air was grave and stately, and his manners were very formal.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Collins's immediate compliments on the beauty of the daughters and his prediction of their marriage are revealed as part of his 'prepared' admiration. This gallantry is not spontaneous but a tactical move in his plan to make 'amends' for the entail. The daughters' discomfort highlights the transactional nature of his praise, which lacks any true appreciation of their individuality.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: doubt her seeing them all in due time well disposed of in marriage.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Collins's detailed examination and praise of the house and furniture betray his mindset as the future owner. His commendations are double-edged, as they remind Mrs. Bennet that everything he admires will eventually be his. This creates a subtle but persistent tension in the domestic space, as the guest acts more like a landlord in training.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: for the mortifying supposition of his viewing it all as his own future property.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The chapter's conclusion with Collins's fifteen-minute apology for a perceived slight about the cook illustrates the absurdity of his social performance. His inability to read the room and his relentless verbal output turn social interaction into a form of endurance for the Bennets. This persistent apologizing serves as a final, defining trait of his overbearing and tiresome character.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: but he continued to apologize for about a quarter of an hour.

quote_entries.speaker: Mr. Bennet
quote_entries.quote: “It is from my cousin, Mr. Collins, who, when I am dead, may turn you all out of this house as soon as he pleases.”

anchor.anchor_text: “It is from my cousin, Mr. Collins, who, when I am dead, may turn you all out of this house as soon as he pleases.”

quote_entries.speaker: Mr. Collins
quote_entries.quote: “I flatter myself that my present overtures of good-will are highly commendable, and that the circumstance of my being next in the entail of Longbourn estate will be kindly overlooked on your side.”

anchor.anchor_text: “I flatter myself that my present overtures of good-will are highly commendable, and that the circumstance of my being next in the entail of Longbourn estate will be kindly overlooked on your side, and not lead you to reject the offered olive branch.”

quote_entries.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quote_entries.quote: “He must be an oddity, I think. I cannot make him out. There is something very pompous in his style.”

anchor.anchor_text: There is something very pompous in his style.

quote_entries.speaker: Mr. Bennet
quote_entries.quote: “No, my dear; I think not. I have great hopes of finding him quite the reverse. There is a mixture of servility and self-importance in his letter which promises well.”

anchor.anchor_text: “No, my dear; I think not. I have great hopes of finding him quite the reverse. There is a mixture of servility and self-importance in his letter which promises well. I am impatient to see him.”

quote_entries.speaker: Mary Bennet
quote_entries.quote: “The idea of the olive branch perhaps is not wholly new, yet I think it is well expressed.”

anchor.anchor_text: “In point of composition,” said Mary, “his letter does not seem defective. The idea of the olive branch perhaps is not wholly new, yet I think it is well expressed.”

quote_entries.speaker: Mr. Collins
quote_entries.quote: “I am very sensible, madam, of the hardship to my fair cousins, and could say much on the subject, but that I am cautious of appearing forward and precipitate.”

anchor.anchor_text: “I am very sensible, madam, of the hardship to my fair cousins, and could say much on the subject, but that I am cautious of appearing forward and precipitate. But I can assure the young ladies that I come prepared to admire them.”

quote_entries.speaker: Mr. Collins
quote_entries.quote: “He begged pardon for having displeased her. In a softened tone she declared herself not at all offended; but he continued to apologize for about a quarter of an hour.”
